title: Measure a tree with a stick
hook: A stick and a tree stand in the same sunlight. Can the stick measure the tree?

knows: ratios and multiplying by a whole number
that a shadow gets longer when the sun is lower
doesNotKnow: that triangles with the same angles have proportional sides

misconception: A longer shadow means adding the extra length to the height (additive), not multiplying.
objective: The learner can explain that the stick and the tree make the same angle with the sun's rays, so height and shadow grow by the same factor: a shadow 7 times longer means a tree 7 times taller.

claims.text: The sun's rays arrive almost parallel, so a stick and a tree at the same moment make the same angle with the ground.
claims.source: The Sun is about 150 million km away, so rays reaching two points metres apart differ in direction by a negligible angle; this is the standard assumption in shadow-measurement problems. The reveal says 'almost'.

claims.text: Triangles with the same angles have the same shape, so height and shadow grow by the same factor: every 3 m of shadow climbs 2 m.
claims.source: AA similarity: equiangular triangles have proportional sides (Euclid, Elements VI.4). The stage draws the staircase of 3-across, 2-up steps under the ray from STICK_S and STICK_H.

claims.text: A 21 m shadow is 7 stick shadows of 3 m, so the tree is 7 × 2 m = 14 m tall.
Adding the extra 18 m of shadow to the stick's 2 m gives 20 m, the wrong answer; the inverted ratio gives 31.5 m.
claims.source: 21 - 3 = 18, 18 + 2 = 20; (3/2) × 21 = 31.5 (recomputed in node). Distractors computed in Demo.tsx from the same constants.

recall.question: A 1.5 m child casts a 2 m shadow. At the same moment a pole casts an 8 m shadow. How tall is the pole?
recall.why: 8 m is 4 times the child's 2 m shadow, so the pole is 4 times the child's height: 4 × 1.5 = 6 m. Adding the extra 6 m gives the wrong 7.5 m.
